talk: Before you sell one more ticket, know what each fan is worth to you. Every fan who walks through the turnstile brings in money and costs you money. What's left over is the only thing that pays for the stadium, the wages and the trophies.

terms.meaning: Profit or loss on one unit of what you sell. Here, one fan at one match.
Price minus the cost that comes with each sale. What one fan 'contributes' to the club.
The point where contribution covers your fixed costs. Zero profit, zero loss.

questions.prompt: A matchday ticket costs $30. Each fan costs you $12 (stewards, cleaning, card fees). What does each fan contribute?
working: That $18 is what you play with. It pays for the stadium, the wages and everything else.
whyNot: That adds the cost to the price: $30 + $12 = $42. Costs come off the price, they don't add to it.
$30 is the ticket price. Some of it goes straight back out on stewards, cleaning and card fees, so you don't keep all of it.
$12 is what each fan costs you, not what they leave behind. Contribution is what's left after that cost: $30 - $12 = $18.

questions.prompt: Running the stadium on matchday costs $90,000 no matter how many fans turn up. How many fans do you need to break even?
questions.hint: Fixed cost divided by contribution per fan.
working: Every fan after the 5,000th is making you money.
whyNot: $90,000 / $30 = 3,000 divides by the ticket price. But each fan costs $12 to host, so only $18 of each ticket goes toward the $90,000.
$90,000 / $12 = 7,500 divides by the cost per fan. Costs don't pay the bills. You need what each fan leaves behind after costs: $18.
9,000 x $18 = $162,000, far more than the $90,000 you need to cover. You break even well before that.

questions.prompt: You normally get 8,000 fans. The commercial team wants a 10% discount, so $27 a ticket. How many EXTRA fans do you need just to make the same profit?
questions.hint: Each fan now leaves $15 instead of $18. Profit today is 8,000 x $18.
working: With the discount each fan leaves $27 - $12 = $15.
1,600 / 8,000 = 20% more fans to cover a 10% discount. Discounts are expensive.
whyNot: 8,000 x 10% = 800 assumes a 10% discount needs 10% more fans. But the $3 comes out of your $18, not the $30 price, so it bites much harder.
9,600 x 10% = 960 mixes up the new crowd with the discount. Compare the new crowd to the old one: 9,600 - 8,000 = 1,600.
A discount only pays for itself if enough new fans come. With the same crowd, 8,000 x $15 = $120,000, and $144,000 - $120,000 = $24,000 short.

penalty.prompt: A ticket costs {price}. Each fan costs {cost} to host, and opening the stadium costs {fixed} a matchday. How many fans do you need to break even?
penalty.hint: Fixed costs divided by what each fan leaves behind.

traps.why: That divides by the ticket price. Each fan only leaves {price - cost|usd} after costs.
That divides by the cost per fan. Divide by what each fan leaves behind: {price - cost|usd}.

call.title: The discount pitch
call.prompt: The commercial team wants 10% off every ticket for the rest of the season, from $30 to $27. They promise 500 more fans a match. Each fan costs $12 to host.

options.label: Approve the discount
options.result: Each fan now leaves $27 - $12 = $15. At 8,000 fans you made 8,000 x $18 = $144,000 a match. Now it's 8,000 + 500 = 8,500 fans, and 8,500 x $15 = $127,500. That's $144,000 - $127,500 = $16,500 less every matchday.

options.label: Say no and keep prices
options.result: Good call. To make the discount pay you'd need 8,000 x $18 / $15 = 9,600 fans, which is 9,600 - 8,000 = 1,600 more, not 500.

options.label: Go bigger: 20% off to fill the ground
options.result: At $30 - $6 = $24 each fan leaves $24 - $12 = $12. With 8,000 + 2,000 = 10,000 fans, 10,000 x $12 = $120,000 a match against $144,000 now. A fuller stadium, and $144,000 - $120,000 = $24,000 less every matchday.

takeaway: Know what one fan leaves behind before you sell one more ticket.
